$comment: Worked dashboards, as reference material for the agent — NOT one-click starting points.
Every query below is written against a schema the person almost certainly does not have.
Applied verbatim, a template is a screen of error messages: the tables do not exist. What
each one is actually worth is the ANSWER to 'which panels belong on this kind of dashboard,
and how are they arranged' — which numbers lead, which chart answers which question, how
many panels before it stops being readable. The agent reads the real schema first and
So: `prompt` is the sentence the person would say, and it is the only part of a template
that can be used as-is — an app may offer these as starting questions. `assumes` names the
tables and columns the SQL was written against, so the agent can see what it is mapping
FROM. `adapt` says what usually differs in a real schema and what to do about it.
`dialect` is postgres throughout. On MySQL, date_trunc('month', x) becomes
DATE_FORMAT(x, '%Y-%m-01'), INTERVAL '30 days' becomes INTERVAL 30 DAY, and FILTER (WHERE
…) becomes SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).
Each `dashboard` is a real, valid schema-1 document — run
skills/dashboard-design/validate_dashboard.py over any of them and it exits clean, so the
examples the agent copies from cannot quietly drift out of the contract.

templates.name: Recurring revenue
templates.description: Where revenue stands, where it moved, and which customers carry it.
templates.prompt: Show me how our recurring revenue is doing — what it is now, how it has moved over the year, and which plans and customers it comes from.

assumes.subscriptions: id, customer_id, plan_id, status, mrr_cents, started_at, canceled_at

templates.adapt: Almost nobody has this schema. What survives is the SHAPE: one row per subscription with a monthly amount, a status, and a start and cancel date. Map onto whatever the real schema calls those — a billing table, a Stripe mirror, an orders table with a recurring flag. Check the real values in `status` before filtering on 'active' (GROUP BY status first). Money is usually an integer of cents: confirm the unit before dividing by 100, and drop the division if the column is already whole currency. If there is no cancellation date anywhere, say so and drop the churn panel rather than inventing it from a status.

queries.name: MRR, customers and average revenue per account, now
queries.sql:
SELECT SUM(mrr_cents) / 100.0 AS mrr,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers,
       AVG(mrr_cents) / 100.0 AS arpa
FROM subscriptions
WHERE status = 'active'

queries.name: Subscription churn, last 30 days
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE canceled_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days') * 100.0
       / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE started_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'), 0)
       AS churn_pct
FROM subscriptions

queries.name: Collected revenue by month, last 12 months
queries.sql:
SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month', paid_at), 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       SUM(amount_cents) / 100.0 AS collected
FROM invoices
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND paid_at >= date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE) - INTERVAL '11 months'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1

queries.name: New and churned MRR by month
queries.sql:
WITH months AS (
  SELECT generate_series(date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE) - INTERVAL '11 months',
                         date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE),
                         INTERVAL '1 month') AS m
)
SELECT to_char(m, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(mrr_cents), 0) / 100.0 FROM subscriptions s
         WHERE date_trunc('month', s.started_at) = m) AS new_mrr,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(mrr_cents), 0) / 100.0 FROM subscriptions s
         WHERE date_trunc('month', s.canceled_at) = m) AS churned_mrr
FROM months
ORDER BY 1

queries.name: Active MRR by plan
queries.sql:
SELECT p.name AS plan,
       SUM(s.mrr_cents) / 100.0 AS mrr
FROM subscriptions s
JOIN plans p ON p.id = s.plan_id
WHERE s.status = 'active'
GROUP BY p.name
ORDER BY 2 DESC

queries.name: Largest active customers
queries.sql:
SELECT c.name AS customer,
       SUM(s.mrr_cents) / 100.0 AS mrr,
       MIN(s.started_at)::date AS customer_since
FROM subscriptions s
JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id
WHERE s.status = 'active'
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY 2 DESC
LIMIT 10

templates.name: Sales pipeline
templates.description: What is in the pipeline, where it stalls, and what is about to close.
templates.prompt: Show me the state of the sales pipeline — how much is open, where deals drop off, how we are converting, and what is closing this month.

assumes.opportunities: id, name, account_id, owner_id, stage, amount_cents, created_at, expected_close_at, closed_at, won

templates.adapt: The shape that matters: one row per deal, with an amount, a stage, an owner, and dates for created / expected close / actually closed. A CRM mirror will have all of it under other names (`deal`, `opportunity`, `pipeline_item`). Two things to check before charting: what the stage column actually contains (GROUP BY stage), and how a won deal is recorded — a boolean, a stage called 'Closed Won', or a status. The funnel panel here orders stages by value, which only approximates the real order; if the schema has a stage rank or probability column, order by that instead so the funnel reads top to bottom the way the team sells.

queries.name: Open pipeline value, deal count and average won size
queries.sql:
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) FILTER (WHERE closed_at IS NULL) / 100.0 AS open_value,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE closed_at IS NULL) AS open_deals,
       AVG(amount_cents) FILTER (WHERE won) / 100.0 AS avg_won_value
FROM opportunities

queries.name: Win rate, deals closed in the last 90 days
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE won) * 100.0 / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) AS win_rate_pct
FROM opportunities
WHERE closed_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'

queries.name: Open pipeline by stage
queries.sql:
SELECT stage,
       COUNT(*) AS deals,
       SUM(amount_cents) / 100.0 AS value
FROM opportunities
WHERE closed_at IS NULL
GROUP BY stage
ORDER BY 3 DESC

queries.name: Deals created and won by week
queries.sql:
SELECT to_char(date_trunc('week', created_at), 'YYYY-MM-DD') AS week,
       COUNT(*) AS created,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE won) AS won_deals
FROM opportunities
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '12 weeks'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1

queries.name: Open pipeline by owner
queries.sql:
SELECT u.name AS owner,
       SUM(o.amount_cents) / 100.0 AS pipeline
FROM opportunities o
JOIN users u ON u.id = o.owner_id
WHERE o.closed_at IS NULL
GROUP BY u.name
ORDER BY 2 DESC
LIMIT 8

queries.name: Open deals expected to close in the next 30 days
queries.sql:
SELECT o.name AS deal,
       a.name AS account,
       o.stage,
       o.amount_cents / 100.0 AS value,
       o.expected_close_at::date AS expected_close
FROM opportunities o
JOIN accounts a ON a.id = o.account_id
WHERE o.closed_at IS NULL
  AND o.expected_close_at <= CURRENT_DATE + INTERVAL '30 days'
ORDER BY o.expected_close_at
LIMIT 10

panels.title: Win rate
panels.caption: Deals closed in the last 90 days

templates.name: Site traffic
templates.description: Who arrived, where from, what they read, and whether they converted.
templates.prompt: Show me site traffic for the last 30 days — sessions and visitors, where they come from, which pages get read, and the conversion rate.

assumes.sessions: id, visitor_id, started_at, utm_source, device, country

templates.adapt: This assumes first-party event tables. Most schemas have something close enough: an events table with a type column, or a page_views table with no separate session row (in which case derive sessions from a session_id column, and drop the visitor stat unless there is a stable visitor id). If conversions are a column on the session rather than their own table, rewrite the conversion query as a COUNT(*) FILTER over that column. 30 days is a choice, not a law — match the window to how often they look at it.

queries.name: Sessions and visitors, last 30 days
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS sessions,
       COUNT(DISTINCT visitor_id) AS visitors
FROM sessions
WHERE started_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'

queries.name: Session conversion rate and depth, last 30 days
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c.session_id) * 100.0 / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT s.id), 0) AS conversion_pct,
       COUNT(v.id) * 1.0 / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT s.id), 0) AS pages_per_session
FROM sessions s
LEFT JOIN conversions c ON c.session_id = s.id
LEFT JOIN page_views v ON v.session_id = s.id
WHERE s.started_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'

queries.name: Sessions by day, last 30 days
queries.sql:
SELECT to_char(date_trunc('day', started_at), 'YYYY-MM-DD') AS day,
       COUNT(*) AS sessions
FROM sessions
WHERE started_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1

queries.name: Sessions by device, last 30 days
queries.sql:
SELECT device,
       COUNT(*) AS sessions
FROM sessions
WHERE started_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY device
ORDER BY 2 DESC

queries.name: Sessions by source, last 30 days
queries.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(utm_source, 'direct') AS source,
       COUNT(*) AS sessions
FROM sessions
WHERE started_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 DESC
LIMIT 8

queries.name: Most read pages, last 30 days
queries.sql:
SELECT path AS page,
       COUNT(*) AS views,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions
FROM page_views
WHERE occurred_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY path
ORDER BY 2 DESC
LIMIT 10

templates.name: Support queue
templates.description: The size of the queue, how fast it is being answered, and what is aging in it.
templates.prompt: Show me how support is doing — how big the queue is, how quickly we answer, whether the backlog is growing, and which tickets have been waiting longest.

assumes.tickets: id, subject, channel, priority, status, created_at, first_response_at, resolved_at, assignee_id

templates.adapt: One row per ticket with three timestamps — created, first answered, resolved — is the whole model; everything here is derived from those. If first_response_at does not exist, the response-time and SLA panels cannot be computed: say that rather than substituting resolution time, which measures something else. The 4-hour SLA below is an assumption — ask what theirs is, or read it from an SLA table if they have one. `good: "down"` on the response-time stat is deliberate: faster is better, and the colour has to know that.

queries.name: Open tickets and how many are still unanswered
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE resolved_at IS NULL) AS open_tickets,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE resolved_at IS NULL AND first_response_at IS NULL) AS unanswered
FROM tickets

queries.name: Median minutes to first reply, last 7 days
queries.sql:
SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (
         ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (first_response_at - created_at)) / 60.0
       ) AS median_first_reply_min
FROM tickets
WHERE first_response_at IS NOT NULL
  AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days'

queries.name: Share answered within four hours, last 7 days
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE first_response_at <= created_at + INTERVAL '4 hours') * 100.0
       / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) AS within_sla_pct
FROM tickets
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days'

queries.name: Tickets opened and resolved by day, last 30 days
queries.sql:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT generate_series(CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '29 days', CURRENT_DATE, INTERVAL '1 day') AS d
)
SELECT to_char(d, 'YYYY-MM-DD') AS day,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets t WHERE date_trunc('day', t.created_at) = d) AS opened,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tickets t WHERE date_trunc('day', t.resolved_at) = d) AS resolved
FROM days
ORDER BY 1

queries.name: Tickets by channel, last 7 days
queries.sql:
SELECT channel,
       COUNT(*) AS tickets
FROM tickets
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days'
GROUP BY channel
ORDER BY 2 DESC

queries.name: Open tickets waiting longest
queries.sql:
SELECT t.subject AS ticket,
       t.channel,
       t.priority,
       ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW() - t.created_at)) / 3600.0) AS hours_waiting
FROM tickets t
WHERE t.resolved_at IS NULL
ORDER BY t.created_at
LIMIT 10

panels.title: Opened and resolved
panels.caption: A gap that stays open is a backlog that is growing

templates.name: Executive summary
templates.description: One number per part of the business, and the two trends behind them.
templates.prompt: Give me a one-screen summary of the business: revenue, new customers, pipeline and support load, plus how revenue and sign-ups have moved this year.
templates.adapt: This one is deliberately thin: four numbers and two trends, because an executive view is read in seconds between meetings. It reaches across four subject areas, so it is the template most likely to need panels REMOVED — if the schema has no CRM tables, three panels is a better dashboard than four with one showing an error. Choose the four numbers with the person: the right four are the ones they would ask about in a board meeting, not the ones that are easiest to query.

queries.name: Recurring revenue now
queries.sql:
SELECT SUM(mrr_cents) / 100.0 AS mrr
FROM subscriptions
WHERE status = 'active'

queries.name: Customers added this month
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS new_customers
FROM customers
WHERE created_at >= date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE)

queries.name: Open pipeline value
queries.sql:
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) / 100.0 AS open_pipeline
FROM opportunities
WHERE closed_at IS NULL

queries.name: Unresolved tickets
queries.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS open_tickets
FROM tickets
WHERE resolved_at IS NULL

queries.name: Collected revenue by month, last 12 months
queries.sql:
SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month', paid_at), 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       SUM(amount_cents) / 100.0 AS collected
FROM invoices
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND paid_at >= date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE) - INTERVAL '11 months'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1

queries.name: New customers by month, last 12 months
queries.sql:
SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month', created_at), 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
WHERE created_at >= date_trunc('month', CURRENT_DATE) - INTERVAL '11 months'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
